think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 74-year-old male with an uneventful total knee arthroplasty performed 4 years earlier presents with a 2-month history of painless, fluctuant prepatellar swelling and a discharging sinus tract extruding straw-colored fluid, without fever, joint pain, or systemic symptoms. The core tension is distinguishing whether this chronic sinus tract represents a superficial acute/chronic pyogenic bursitis (e.g. Staphylococcus aureus), a deep periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) threatening the prosthetic implant, crystal arthropathy (gout/pseudogout), or an indolent tuberculous bursitis sparing the joint.
2. Admission Breakpoint: Initial presentation and triage after clinical examination of the knee, baseline blood work (CBC, ESR, CRP), plain knee radiographs, and needle aspiration yielding bursal fluid. Confirmatory microbiological testing (Ziehl-Neelsen stain, mycobacterial cultures, bone scan, and PPD) begins after this point.
3. Differential Distinctions: Deep PJI was ruled out by preserved range of motion (5-110 deg), lack of joint effusion, normal bone-prosthesis interface without osteolysis on radiographs, and normal uptake on triple-phase bone scan. Pyogenic bacterial bursitis was excluded by the painless, afebrile, 2-month indolent course, normal fluid cell counts, and sterile bacterial cultures. Gout was excluded by the absence of crystals. Tuberculous bursitis was established by acid-fast bacilli on ZN stain and culture isolation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
case_prompt:
A 74-year-old male retired teacher presented with a 2-month history of a gradually developing, painless swelling over the anterior aspect of his left knee, associated with a small cutaneous sinus that was extruding straw-colored fluid. Four years earlier, he had undergone an uneventful left total knee arthroplasty (TKA) for degenerative osteoarthritis, with no history of delayed wound healing or persistent drainage. He had no history of fever, chills, anorexia, weight loss, recent trauma, travel, or occupational kneeling activities. His medical history was notable only for well-controlled hypertension. He was ambulatory with the assistance of a cane.
On physical examination, general parameters and vital signs were within normal limits. Positive physical findings were confined to the left knee, where there was an anterior prepatellar swelling measuring approximately 7 cm in diameter, which was fluctuant and non-tender to palpation, with minimal surrounding erythema localized chiefly to a punctum. Pressure over the punctum expressed yellowish discharge. There was no bony tenderness over the patella, distal femur, or proximal tibia. No intra-articular knee effusion, joint instability, or crepitus was present. Active range of motion was well preserved (5° to 110°), with mild discomfort elicited only at terminal flexion due to compression of the prepatellar bursa.
Laboratory evaluation revealed normal total and differential white blood cell counts, a slightly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 80 mm/hr (normal: 30-70 mm/hr), and a slightly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) level of 8 mg/L (normal: 0-4 mg/L). Plain radiographs of the knee demonstrated prepatellar soft-tissue swelling with no evidence of osteolysis, periosteal reaction, or loosening at the bone-prosthesis interface. Needle aspiration of the prepatellar bursa yielded 50 mL of slightly turbid, straw-colored yellowish fluid.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Acute or chronic pyogenic bacterial bursitis (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because prepatellar bursal collections with draining cutaneous sinuses are most commonly pyogenic in origin. However, the patient's presentation was indolent, completely painless, and afebrile, and aspirated bursal fluid revealed normal cell counts, no organisms on Gram stain, and sterile bacterial cultures.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Aspiration results revealed normal cell counts, no crystals, and no organisms on Gram stain.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Deep periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) / prosthetic hardware loosening
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the presence of a draining sinus tract in close proximity to an in situ total knee arthroplasty. However, the patient maintained a full range of motion without intra-articular effusion, plain radiographs demonstrated no bone-prosthesis interface loosening or osteolysis, and a three-phase bone scan showed normal uptake.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: There were no obvious bony changes, osteolysis, or loosening at the bone-prosthesis interface.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The pivotal clinical and microbiological turning point was Ziehl-Neelsen staining of the aspirated bursal fluid demonstrating acid-fast bacilli, subsequently confirmed on culture as Mycobacterium tuberculosis sensitive to first-line agents, establishing isolated tuberculous prepatellar bursitis sparing the prosthetic knee.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: To our surprise, ZN stain revealed acid-fast bacilli consistent with typical tuberculous infection; the bacterium was confirmed on culture 6 weeks later as Mycobacterium tuberculosis-sensitive to rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and streptomycin.

editor_comments: Verified admission breakpoint strictly excludes ZN stain, mycobacterial cultures, bone scan, PPD test, and antitubercular treatment.
